researchPapers.title: Bull Shark (Carcharhinus leucas) Occurrence along Beaches of South-Eastern Australia: Understanding Where, When, and Why
keyFindings: Bull Sharks are THE primary species responsible for the overwhelming majority of shark incidents in Sydney - 86% of bites occur in estuaries/freshwater
Recent spate of Sydney attacks were all Bull Sharks - they dominate Sydney harbour and river systems
Rainfall events are a critical driver - Bull Sharks actively move into estuarine and coastal areas after significant rainfall (>30-40mm)
Water temperature above 18-20°C correlates with increased Bull Shark presence in nearshore zones
Bull Sharks are attracted to areas with reduced salinity (river mouths, harbours) especially post-rainfall
Summer-autumn period (Nov-Apr) shows peak activity in Sydney, particularly in harbour locations
Turbid/murky water conditions from runoff actually attract Bull Sharks as they hunt effectively using electroreception

researchPapers.title: Increased shark bite survivability revealed by two centuries of Australian records
keyFindings: 86% of Bull Shark bites occurred in estuarine and freshwater systems in Australia
Bull Sharks dominate Sydney attacks - particularly in harbour and river systems (1900-1963 Sydney estuaries)
White Sharks are primarily found in cooler southern Australian waters (Victoria, South Australia, Tasmania)
Bull Shark survivability is 62%, Tiger Shark 75%, White Shark 53%
Tiger Sharks prefer warmer northern waters - uncommon in temperate regions like Sydney
On-water activities (surfing, kayaking) show 88-92% survivability vs 30-45% for in-water activities (swimming, diving)
Time between injury and treatment is crucial for survival - rapid first aid significantly improves outcomes

researchPapers.title: Environmental determinants of shark attacks: a review of published data
keyFindings: Water temperature is a significant predictor of shark presence in temperate coastal zones
Seasonal patterns show increased activity during warmer months (Nov-Feb in Southern Hemisphere)
Turbidity from runoff reduces visibility and may increase encounter risk

researchPapers.title: Shark behaviour and ecology in response to environmental variation
keyFindings: Temperature drives seasonal migration patterns for multiple shark species
Nearshore movements increase with water temperatures above 20°C
Environmental fluctuations correlate with changes in habitat use

researchPapers.title: Global patterns and predictions of seafloor biomass using random forests
keyFindings: Swell and wave action influence nearshore prey availability
Moderate swell conditions (1.5-3m) associated with increased predator activity in surf zones

researchPapers.title: Coastal urbanization and marine predator-prey dynamics
keyFindings: Rainfall events increase nutrient runoff, affecting coastal prey distribution
Turbidity from storm water discharge may mask visual predator cues
Urban coastal zones show distinct environmental risk patterns

researchPapers.title: Shark movement patterns and environmental drivers in temperate coastal waters
keyFindings: Sharks exhibit predictable responses to temperature gradients
Summer months correlate with increased nearshore presence
Water quality and visibility impact predator foraging efficiency

researchPapers.title: Environmental factors influencing shark bite incidents
keyFindings: Combination of environmental factors better predicts risk than single variables
Rainfall preceding beach activity increases turbidity and reduces water clarity
Seasonal water temperature is the strongest single predictor

dataProvenance.description: Daily rainfall totals from Sydney Observatory Hill (Station 066062) and regional observation stations
Sea surface temperature from Sydney offshore buoys and coastal stations (Fort Denison and Sydney offshore observations)
Significant wave height from offshore observation buoys in the Sydney region
Water quality is estimated as a proxy based on recent rainfall. Heavy rainfall (>45mm in 48h) is assumed to cause runoff and reduced water clarity/increased turbidity.

disclaimer: This system provides an environmental risk assessment based on known correlations between weather/ocean conditions and shark activity patterns from peer-reviewed research. It is NOT a shark detection or sighting system. The risk levels are heuristic estimates and should be used in conjunction with official beach safety information, lifeguard warnings, and personal judgement. Always swim at patrolled beaches, follow local signage, and never swim alone. The Bureau of Meteorology data used is provided 'as-is' and may be subject to delays or outages.

methodology.overview: This system implements a multi-species shark risk assessment model based on peer-reviewed research. Each shark species is scored independently using its own environmental model, thresholds, and weights. The overall risk represents the weighted combination of all species present, taking into account their likelihood and incident history at each specific location.

rainfall.rationale: PRIMARY DRIVER - Bull Sharks actively move into estuarine areas after rainfall, seeking reduced salinity

turbidity.rationale: Attracted to turbid water - hunt using electroreception, not vision

temperature.rationale: Active at lower temperatures than most species

swell.rationale: Less relevant - prefer calmer estuarine waters

season.rationale: Peak in summer but present year-round

location.rationale: Strong habitat preference for low-salinity environments

speciesModels.sydneyRelevance: PRIMARY THREAT - Responsible for overwhelming majority of Sydney attacks, especially in harbour and river systems

speciesModels.habitat: Cooler open ocean, southern Australian waters

temperature.rationale: Prefer cooler water than other species

swell.rationale: Tolerates higher swell in open ocean

turbidity.rationale: Visual hunter - prefer clear water (opposite of Bull Sharks)

speciesModels.sydneyRelevance: RARE - White Sharks prefer cooler southern Australian waters (Victoria, SA, Tasmania). Extremely uncommon in Sydney region

swell.rationale: Most active in surf zones with moderate swell

location.rationale: Prefer surf zones at open beaches

speciesModels.sydneyRelevance: COMMON but LOW DANGER - Frequently present in Sydney surf zones but rarely involved in serious incidents

temperature.rationale: Warm water species - requires higher temperatures

location.rationale: Sydney is at southern edge of range - 30% reduction applied

speciesModels.sydneyRelevance: RARE - Tiger Sharks prefer warmer northern Australian waters. Uncommon in temperate Sydney

methodology.overallScoring: Each species is scored independently (0-100) based on current environmental conditions. Species scores are then weighted by: (1) Species likelihood at location (common=1.0x, occasional=0.6x, rare=0.3x), and (2) Incident history (high=1.0x, moderate=0.7x, low=0.4x). The weighted average determines overall risk. Final scores map to: Low (0-20), Moderate (21-40), High (41-60), Severe (61-80), Catastrophic (81-100).
methodology.locationGuidance: Based on current risk conditions, we recommend swimming at patrolled open ocean beaches (Bondi, Coogee, Maroubra) rather than harbour/estuary locations. Avoid swimming in Sydney Harbour, river mouths, and estuaries especially after rainfall. Bull Sharks dominate Sydney attacks and are most active in harbour/estuarine environments after rainfall events.
